nodes.label: Tragedy of the Commons
nodes.summary: Hardin: shared open pasture is overgrazed because each herder gains fully but shares the cost.
nodes.details:
- Garrett Hardin pictures a **pasture open to all**.
- Each herder adds animals: **gain is private**, **cost of overgrazing is shared**.
- Rational individual choices lead to collective ruin.
- The idea is *debated*: literature says commons means **shared ownership** with rules, not open access.

nodes.label: Open-access resources
nodes.summary: Renewable resources owned by no one, so nobody can exclude users: prone to overuse.
nodes.details:
Open-access resources are **not owned by anyone**; access is free, so use is unrestricted.

- Examples: fisheries in the high seas, atmosphere.
- Contrast with **commons** governed by community rules.

nodes.label: Customary forest Barambang Katute
nodes.summary: Indonesian customary forest managed by community rules: a commons that avoids the tragedy.
nodes.details:
A customary (**adat**) forest governed by local institutions shows that shared ownership with **rules and sanctions** can sustain a resource.

- Contradicts the idea that commons always fail.

nodes.label: Planetary Boundaries
nodes.summary: Nine Earth-system limits within which humanity can operate safely.
nodes.details:
The **planetary boundaries** framework defines a safe operating space for humanity across nine Earth-system processes (climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen/phosphorus flows, land-system change, etc.).

- Crossing a boundary risks abrupt, irreversible change.
- Several are already transgressed.
nodes.examTips: Know that boundaries are interlinked and some are already exceeded.

nodes.label: Climate change boundary
nodes.summary: One of the boundaries, quantified by atmospheric CO2 and radiative forcing.
nodes.details: Climate change is one of the control variables; it connects to the GHG material of week 6.

nodes.label: 3.1 Carrying capacity & population
nodes.summary: Limits to population growth: carrying capacity, Malthus, Neo-Malthus, Kerala.
nodes.details: Section 3.1 explores whether population growth is bounded by the environment.

nodes.label: Environmental carrying capacity
nodes.summary: Maximum population an environment can sustain given limiting factors.
nodes.details:
There is **always a limit** to population growth. Limiting factors include food, water, space and energy.

- Growth beyond carrying capacity leads to decline.
- Technology can shift (not remove) the limit.

nodes.label: Malthusian view
nodes.summary: Population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, causing checks on growth.
nodes.details:
Malthus argued that **population outpaces resources**, causing famine and disease as natural checks.

- Pessimistic view of unchecked population growth.

nodes.label: Neo-Malthusian theorem
nodes.summary: Updated Malthusian concern including environmental degradation; technology may postpone limits.
nodes.details: Neo-Malthusians connect population to **resource depletion and pollution**. Slides discuss the role of technology and agriculture in extending limits.

nodes.label: Case study: Kerala, India
nodes.summary: Kerala lowered fertility through education and health rather than coercion.
nodes.details: Kerala shows population limits are an **effect rather than a cause**: social development (female education, healthcare) reduced growth.

nodes.label: 3.2 Impact: IPAT & technology
nodes.summary: From population to environmental impact; the IPAT identity and the dual role of technology.
nodes.details: Section 3.2 links people, wealth and technology to impact.

nodes.label: IPAT equation
nodes.summary: I = P × A × T: impact is population times affluence times technology.
nodes.details:
**I = P × A × T**

- **P**: population size
- **A**: affluence (consumption per person)
- **T**: technology (impact per unit of consumption)

Impact depends on all three, not just population.
nodes.examTips: Explain why T can increase OR decrease I.

nodes.label: Technology factor (T)
nodes.summary: T can reduce impact via efficiency or raise it via new consumption.
nodes.details: See the dual role of technology.

nodes.label: Dual role of technology
nodes.summary: Technology improves efficiency but can also enable greater consumption (rebound).
nodes.details: Technology **improves efficiency** in use and management of natural resources, yet progress also **drives consumption patterns** upward.

nodes.label: Environmental justice
nodes.summary: Environmental burdens fall unequally: EV batteries and AI data centers shift impacts to others.
nodes.details: Unequal impacts: producers of materials (e.g. for **EV batteries**) bear pollution; **data centers for AI** consume water and energy.

nodes.label: 3.3 Over- and hyper-consumption
nodes.summary: Consumption beyond needs and its environmental toll.
nodes.details: Section 3.3 covers overconsumption concepts.

nodes.label: Overconsumption
nodes.summary: Consuming beyond what is needed or what the Earth can regenerate.
nodes.details: Overconsumption relates to **addiction-like** consumption patterns and large per-capita CO2 in rich countries.

nodes.label: Hyperconsumption
nodes.summary: Consumption driven by identity, status and marketing rather than need.
nodes.details: Hyperconsumption extends overconsumption: buying as culture.

nodes.label: 3.4 Ecological footprint
nodes.summary: Measuring human demand on nature against biocapacity.
nodes.details: Section 3.4 measures consumption in global hectares.

nodes.label: Ecological footprint
nodes.summary: Area of productive land and sea needed to supply resources and absorb wastes.
nodes.details: The **ecological footprint** converts consumption into area. If everyone lived like some nations, we would need **multiple Earths**.

nodes.label: 6.1 Climate change & SDGs
nodes.summary: What climate change is, GHGs, and links between SDG 13 and other SDGs.
nodes.details: Section 6.1.

nodes.label: Climate change
nodes.summary: Long-term shift in average atmospheric conditions of a region.
nodes.details: Climate is the **average atmospheric condition** over a long period. Climate change is a persistent change in it.

nodes.label: Greenhouse gases
nodes.summary: Gases that absorb heat energy radiated from Earth, warming the atmosphere.
nodes.details: GHGs absorb heat. Concentrations have increased over time; excess GHG causes **global warming**.

nodes.label: SDG 13 and other SDGs
nodes.summary: Climate action both affects and depends on progress on other SDGs.
nodes.details: Slides map how SDG 13 contributes to others and vice versa.

nodes.label: 6.2 Paris Agreement & Indonesia
nodes.summary: The 2015-2030 Paris Agreement, its principles and Indonesia's commitment.
nodes.details: Section 6.2.

nodes.label: Paris Agreement
nodes.summary: 2015 global agreement to limit warming; countries submit nationally determined contributions.
nodes.details: Core principles: **equity (CBDR-RC)**, **transparency** (global stocktake) and **sovereignty**.

nodes.label: CBDR-RC
nodes.summary: Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
nodes.details: All countries share responsibility, but **differ by historical contribution and capability**. Linked to the 'right to development'.
nodes.examTips: Why does CBDR matter for the Global South?

nodes.label: Transparency & global stocktake
nodes.summary: Periodic review of collective progress ratchets ambition.
nodes.details: The **Global Stocktake** assesses collective progress.

nodes.label: Indonesia 2nd NDC (2025)
nodes.summary: Indonesia's updated pledge responding to the first global stocktake, with emissions peaking by 2030.
nodes.details: Scenarios show emissions **peaking in 2030** before dropping toward net zero.

nodes.label: 6.4 What can we do?
nodes.summary: Mitigation: peatlands, AFOLU and reducing GHG impacts.
nodes.details: Section 6.4.

nodes.label: Tropical peatlands
nodes.summary: Carbon-rich wetlands; drainage and fires release huge emissions in Indonesia.
nodes.details: Peatland carbon cycle, disturbance and **fires** matter for Indonesia's emissions.

nodes.label: AFOLU
nodes.summary: Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use: sector for reducing GHG impacts.
nodes.details: Reducing GHGs from AFOLU is a key mitigation lever.
